Against Oblivion: The Moral and Practical Case Against a ‘Right to Be Forgotten’

Introduction
Every shred of information on the public Internet—news articles, public-records databases, blog posts, court filings, social-media archives—is a brick in an ever-growing global memory structure. Recent European jurisprudence has asserted a quasi-constitutional “right to be forgotten” (RtBF) that empowers courts and regulators to order removal of lawful but “inadequate, irrelevant or no longer relevant” materials. Such a prerogative is marketed as compassionate privacy protection; in reality it is history-erasing censorship that erodes individual autonomy, distorts collective memory, and corrodes liberal democratic order. Supporters portray it as a shield for the vulnerable; critics see it as a license for elites and wrongdoers to whitewash public records. This essay explains why unrestricted preservation of historical online information is not merely a technical necessity, but a moral imperative, and why RtBF laws should be repealed or, at a minimum, dramatically narrowed.

  1. Knowledge Should Be Immutable Once Lawfully Published
    a. Public records are not private data. A civil-court judgment, bankrupt-cy filing, professional misconduct finding, or newspaper exposé exists precisely because its disclosure serves a broader public interest. Labeling truthful, legitimately disseminated material “private” retroactively is an intellectual sleight-of-hand.
    b. Memory is the fundamental prerequisite of accountability. To debate, aggregate, and learn from the past requires that the past remain available. If the record can be selectively censored at the behest of interested parties, the very concept of accountability is emasculated. History disappears into a mediated redaction.

  2. RtBF Empowers the Powerful, Hurts the Public
    a. Litigation is unevenly distributed. The well-lawyered will systematically reach for erasure; the poor or politically unpopular will lack resources to fight back. Thus banks or reputational-PR firms become day-to-day custodians of what society is permitted to remember.
    b. A tool for predators. Stalkers, swindlers, disgraced executives, and corrupt officials already use takedown notices to expunge articles documenting accusations or convictions. RtBF normalizes而不是eliminates their tactics.
    c. Chilling side effects on investigative journalism. If every publisher must build a budget item for eventual delisting requests, editors may choose pre-emptive exclusion of marginal yet newsworthy material rather than risk later legal battles.

  3. Search Engines as Essential Public Utilities, Not Memory Prisons
    The European Court of Justice’s Google Spain decision placed liability on search engines instead of publishers for index accuracy. This is at once perverse and counter-constitutional: treating the librarian as liable for the book’s contents. Given that search engines are overwhelmingly how researchers navigate knowledge, removing URLs amounts to digitalbook-burning. A democratically accountable society does not countenance a Ministry of Indexing empowered to scribble through yesterday.

  4. “Irrelevance” Is Subjective and Corruptible
    “Outdated,” “irrelevant,” “excessive” are hazy standards inviting limitless litigation. A bankrupt CEO may wish a 15-year-old SEC filing irrelevant; a fraud victim researching lenders will view it as intensely relevant. Prudence demands that relevance is determined by the reader-chooser, not by claimant-appointed arbiters or black-box algorithms.

  5. Slippery Slope and International Contagion
    After their 2014 ruling, Google removed articles about right-wing politicians convicted of tax fraud in Spain, German doctors involved in malpractice suits, and even an article describing the physical abuse of a nanny by celebrities. One can easily foresee authoritarian regimes pleading RtBF to purge references to disappeared dissidents, to genocidal crimes, or to real-estate scandals that implicate ruling families. “European privacy” quickly becomes global memory gag. Russia has already copied the mechanism to erase politically embarrassing links.

  6. No Effective Technical Firewall Exists
    a. Extraterritorial reach. The Court of Justice of the EU grants rights-hol-ders power to force delisting on a worldwide basis (Canada’s Supreme Court and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner mimic such demands). A server in California is no safe haven from judgment handed down in Luxembourg.
    b. Database consolidation and inevitable leakage. Once a right to erase is recognized, pressure mounts to remove data not only from search-results snippets but from archives (public-records aggregators, Internet Archive, newspaper databases). There is no principled legal stopping point between URL delisting and wholesale bleachbitting.

  7. Ascendant Counter-Technologies Make RtBF Futile as Well as Wrong
    a. Cryptographic permanence. IPFS, Ethereum Name Service, steganographically embedded torrent hashes, blockchain ledgers—technologies premised on tamper-proof content addressing—render obliteration impossible in practice.
    b. Mirrors and dark archives spring up automatically when deletions are publicized (Streisand effect). Legal deletion therefore redistributes, ratherthan destroys, the data, while garbling the trail of authenticity.

  8. Negative Externalities on Social Science and AI Safety
    History is a public good. Economists and epidemiologists mine Google Trends to trace contagion patterns; policy researchers use bankruptcy registries to target consumer-protection reforms. Every arbitrary erasure is a permanent hole punched in empirical datasets, thereby stunting knowledge.

  9. The Privacy Red Herring
    a. Actual identified private data (e.g., Social Security numbers, home addresses within news stories) is already protected by separate laws that mandate removal. RtBF tackles truthful reporting in the public interest—then masquerades as privacy defense.
    b. Voluntary solutions abound without coercion: the individual may seek a correction or update from news outlets, issue a rebuttal statement, or build new digital visibility indexed under fresh keywords. These tools, unlike compelled censorship, leave no collateral damage on the commons.

  10. Moral and Philosophical Foundations
    a. Liberal societies traditionally place severe burdens on speech restriction: speech must pose a clear and present danger (Brandenburg v. Ohio). European RtBF denies this standard by subjecting mere “harm to social image” to state erasure.
    b. Personhood depends on remembering; amnesia is not healing. Oblivion does not rehabilitate, it infantilizes—treating citizens as too fragile to bear their own biographies. Maturity means owning one’s past, not petitioning the state to re-author it. As Santayana warned, those who forget the past are condemned to repeat it; societies that legally enforce forgetting are worse—they condemn everyone else to repeat another’s sin unknowingly.

  11. The Fallacy of the “Eternal Footprint” Problem
    Pro-search critics often caricature unrestricted retention as condemning a teenager who posted an edgy joke at 15 to lifelong ostracism. Yet: (1) contextual nuance and forgiveness are becoming social norms as digital natives occupy positions of authority themselves; (2) employment law and human-resources norms evolve faster than legislation; (3) new norms of data opacity are emerging (e.g., expungement of juvenile criminal records is a useful but narrowly targeted exception). Society already owns calibration tools for extreme harms without enshrining a general censorship right.

  12. Alternatives to RtBF Enhancement—Rebuttal and Context
    Rather than delete public truth, society should double down on provenance, proven truthful correction, and algorithmic context windows. Projects such as the Credibility Coalition and WhatWasIntended metadata add contextual annotations, timestamps, updates, and fact-checks without deleting the original article. These methods acknowledge human complexity without rewriting history.

Conclusion
A patch of sunlight extinguished from the digital commons is a metabook yanked forever from the public shelf. Once granted, the power to erase dissolves trust in every subsequently curated archive. Transparency about healthy debate becomes transparency only after privileged excision. In a world where information abundance already fragments collective attention, the one corrective we possess is reliable, indexed memory. The “right to be forgotten” is not about protecting fragile privacy; it is about the strong demanding revisionist opacity at the expense of the many. Upholding a norm of unrestricted access to publicly published knowledge is therefore a bulwark for liberal governance, a safeguard against elite manipulation, and a moral commitment to preserve the enduring conversation of humankind. To forget—especially by coercive legal mandate—is not merely to forgive; it is to betray future generations owed unredacted history.

The Right to Be Forgotten Undermines History, Free Inquiry, and Personal Accountability

The "right to be forgotten," codified in European Union data protection rules and extended through court cases like the 2014 Google Spain decision, allows individuals to demand that search engines delist links to publicly available information about them when it is deemed "inadequate, irrelevant, or excessive." Proponents frame this as a privacy safeguard against perpetual embarrassment or outdated harms. The position collapses under scrutiny. Removing or hiding links to factual, once-public records from search indexes does not erase history or protect dignity; it distorts collective memory, weakens democratic accountability, and substitutes bureaucratic gatekeeping for open access to verifiable information.

Public records and online content published without legal restriction represent voluntary exposure or necessary societal documentation. Articles about court convictions, business dealings, public statements, professional conduct, or events reported at the time exist in the world precisely because they mattered to publishers, readers, and participants. Delisting them from search results does not prevent motivated researchers from locating the original pages through archives, browser caches, direct URLs, or alternative engines. It merely burdens ordinary users—voters checking a candidate's record, employers verifying credentials, journalists tracing patterns, or citizens trying to understand community events—with incomplete search results. The information remains "out there," but the most efficient discovery mechanism is censored. This creates a two-tier knowledge system: full access for the technically adept or persistent, filtered access for everyone else.

Historical integrity suffers most directly. Societies that scrub inconvenient pasts repeat mistakes or enable revisionism. Official or quasi-official delisting mimics analog precedents of selective memory—burning libraries, airbrushing photographs, or excising names from encyclopedias—by rendering uncomfortable facts harder to find without proving they never existed. A business owner's prior bankruptcy, a politician's earlier contradictory stance, or a public figure's documented misconduct becomes harder to surface in real time. Over generations, this fragments the factual base on which institutions, elections, and cultural understanding rest. Unrestricted indexing, by contrast, preserves a chronological trail: economic missteps inform investment decisions; prior crimes or frauds guide risk assessments; evolving views on policy can be weighed against consistency rather than claims of redemption.

Accountability erodes when individuals treat past actions as optional biographical chapters subject to legal veto. Public scrutiny disciplines behavior. A physician with malpractice history, a contractor with consumer complaints, or an activist with recorded inflammatory statements gains leverage to sanitize results, while victims, regulators, or counterparties lose easy discovery. This incentive structure favors short-term reputation management over long-term consistency. Laws already address defamation, privacy invasion, harassment, or fraud through targeted civil remedies requiring proof of falsity or harm before a judge. Broad "forgetting" powers bypass those standards, granting preemptive erasure authority to private data subjects rather than neutral adjudication.

Enforcement problems compound the issue. Search engines operate globally; compliance with one jurisdiction's demands can trigger requests elsewhere, inviting forum shopping or reciprocal censorship. Governments or influential complainants hold asymmetric power to initiate delisting, while counter-interest groups or average citizens rarely match resources to challenge it. Criteria for "inadequate, irrelevant, or excessive" invite subjective judgment: relevance shifts with time, context, and culture. What appears outdated to one person supplies essential context to another. Delegating line-drawing to corporations under penalty of fines or to overburdened regulators replaces transparent public debate with opaque administrative processes.

Proponents' counterarguments—persistent stigma from youthful errors, revenge porn lasting effects, or disproportionate harm to ordinary people—do not justify content removal. They justify different tools. Individuals retain primary responsibility for what they publish or tolerate publication of. The Case for Unrestricted Access: Why Right to be Forgotten Laws Undermine the Public Interest

Introduction

The emergence of digital technology has fundamentally transformed how information is created, stored, and retrieved. In this new landscape, several jurisdictions—most prominently the European Union—have implemented "Right to be Forgotten" laws, granting individuals the legal right to request the removal of personal information from search engine results and, in some cases, from websites themselves. While these laws emerge from legitimate concerns about privacy and dignity, they represent a dangerous encroachment on fundamental principles of free expression, historical accuracy, and the public's right to access information. This essay argues that such laws should be opposed in favor of maintaining unrestricted access to historical online information, as the benefits of open information access substantially outweigh the privacy interests these laws purport to protect.

The Historical Imperative of Record-Keeping

The preservation of accurate historical records represents one of civilization's most important achievements. Libraries, archives, and historical societies have long served as custodians of collective memory, enabling societies to learn from past mistakes, hold powerful entities accountable, and understand the trajectory of human progress. The internet, in this sense, represents merely the latest iteration of this ancient impulse toward documentation.

Before digital technology, information about individuals was substantially more difficult to access, but the principle remained that public records, newspaper accounts, and historical documents remained available to those who sought them. A person's criminal history, professional accomplishments, financial dealings, and public statements were, in principle, discoverable by anyone with sufficient motivation to research them. The Right to be Forgotten laws fundamentally alter this paradigm, creating a legal mechanism by which individuals can effectively rewrite their digital history—a power that was never available in the analog age.

Freedom of Information and the Public's Right to Know

At the core of this debate lies a fundamental tension between individual privacy and the public's right to access information. The arguments for unrestricted access draw heavily on principles of free expression and the public's interest in knowing about individuals with whom they interact professionally, personally, or politically.

When individuals operate in public spaces—whether as business professionals, elected officials, community leaders, or simply as participants in public discourse—they forfeit certain expectations of privacy. A person who has been convicted of a crime, engaged in professional misconduct, made controversial public statements, or been involved in public controversies has participated in events of public concern. The ability to search for and discover information about such past events enables citizens to make informed decisions about whom to trust, employ, vote for, or otherwise engage with.

Consider the implications of a system in which employers cannot discover that a job candidate was previously fired for misconduct, in which investors cannot find information about a business partner's previous bankruptcies, or in which voters cannot access information about a candidate's past positions or controversies. The Right to be Forgotten, in practice, creates a two-tiered system of information access: sophisticated actors who know where to look can often find removed information through archival services, specialized databases, or international search engines, while ordinary citizens are left with incomplete and potentially misleading information.

Accountability and the Deterrent Effect of Public Records

One of the most important functions of unrestricted information access is its role in deterring misconduct. The knowledge that actions may be permanently recorded and discoverable exerts a moderating influence on behavior. Individuals and organizations are more likely to act ethically when they understand that their actions may be scrutinized not just at the moment of occurrence but indefinitely into the future.

This accountability function extends to powerful institutions as well as individuals. Corporations that know their environmental violations, labor practices, or financial dealings may be permanently discoverable have stronger incentives to operate responsibly. Public officials who understand that their votes, statements, and decisions will remain accessible face greater accountability than those who can rely on eventual information removal.

The Right to be Forgotten effectively grants a permanent "clean slate" to individuals who might otherwise face ongoing consequences for their actions. While rehabilitation and second chances represent noble values, the legal erasure of historical information removes the ability of the public to make their own judgments about an individual's trustworthiness based on past conduct. A person who was defrauded in a business transaction, victimized by an abuser, or harmed by professional misconduct retains a legitimate interest in others being able to discover information about the perpetrator's history.

Journalistic Integrity and Historical Accuracy

A robust free press depends on the ability to access and publish historical information. Investigative journalism frequently relies on the accumulation of publicly available records to identify patterns of behavior, expose corruption, and hold powerful actors accountable. The removal of information from search engines and websites undermines this function by making it substantially more difficult to piece together comprehensive portraits of individuals and institutions.

Historical accuracy requires the preservation of primary source materials. If individuals can successfully petition for the removal of information they find embarrassing or damaging, the historical record becomes not only incomplete but actively misleading. Future researchers, journalists, and ordinary citizens seeking to understand past events will encounter a sanitized version of history that reflects not what actually happened but what powerful actors wished to conceal.

The digital age has not diminished these concerns; it has amplified them. The internet enables unprecedented access to information, and the corresponding ability to search historical records represents a democratic advancement that should be preserved rather than curtailed. While privacy concerns are legitimate, they can be addressed through other means—defamation law, data protection regulations governing collection and use, and individual choices about what information to share—without resort to information deletion.

The Practical Limitations and Unintended Consequences

Beyond the principled arguments against Right to be Forgotten laws, practical considerations reveal significant limitations in their implementation and troubling unintended consequences.

First, these laws create substantial enforcement challenges in a global internet. An individual in one jurisdiction may successfully obtain removal of information from search engines operating in that jurisdiction, but the underlying information often remains accessible through international search engines, archived versions of websites, or simple screenshots. The result is a system that primarily affects ordinary citizens while sophisticated actors bypass restrictions entirely.

Second, Right to be Forgotten laws create perverse incentives. Individuals and organizations may deliberately obscure negative information through legal threats and removal requests, making it more difficult to identify patterns of problematic behavior. A business with a history of consumer fraud might systematically remove negative press coverage, leaving future customers without warning signs that would be visible to someone conducting research in an unrestricted information environment.

Third, these laws create difficult line-drawing problems. If past crimes can be removed from search results, what about past accusations? If professional misconduct can be erased, what about academic dishonesty? If controversial political statements can be deleted, what about any public statement an individual later regrets? The subjective nature of these determinations inevitably leads to inconsistent application and the potential for abuse.

Addressing Legitimate Privacy Concerns Through Alternative Means

The arguments presented here do not deny the legitimacy of privacy concerns. Individuals do have legitimate interests in protecting certain categories of personal information, and society has developed various mechanisms for balancing these interests against other values.

Data protection regulations that govern how organizations collect, store, and use personal information can address many privacy concerns without deleting historical records. Individuals can choose what information to share online and can work with platforms to restrict access to certain categories of sensitive data. Employers and other entities can be subject to regulations limiting how they use certain types of historical information in decision-making.

The special case of certain categories of information—particularly information about victims of crimes, personal health information, and information about minors—may warrant specific protections. However, these concerns can be addressed through targeted regulations rather than broad-based information removal that affects all categories of historical data.

Conclusion

The push toward Right to be Forgotten laws reflects understandable concerns about privacy in the digital age, but the cure is worse than the disease. Unrestricted access to historical online information serves essential functions in democratic societies: enabling accountability, preserving historical accuracy, supporting investigative journalism, and empowering individuals to make informed decisions about those with whom they interact.

The public interest in accessing information about past events—particularly events of public concern involving public figures, businesses seeking to engage with consumers, or individuals whose past conduct may be relevant to current relationships—substantially outweighs the privacy interests that Right to be Forgotten laws attempt to protect. While privacy concerns are legitimate and should be addressed through other means, the permanent deletion of historical records represents an unacceptable infringement on fundamental principles of free expression and the public's right to know.

Rather than retreating into a sanitized digital landscape where only the powerful can access complete information, societies should embrace the unprecedented opportunity the internet provides for historical documentation and access. The ability to search, discover, and learn from past events represents one of the great advances of the information age—a capability that should be preserved rather than undermined by well-intentioned but ultimately counterproductive regulations.

The Case Against the Right to Be Forgotten: Preserving Transparency, History, and Information Freedom

The Right to be Forgotten (RTBF) legislation, which allows individuals to request the removal of personal information from online platforms, represents one of the most contentious debates in contemporary digital policy. While proponents argue that such legislation empowers individuals to control their digital identities and protects them from lasting harm caused by outdated or irrelevant information, a compelling counterargument exists: the permanent retention of public online records serves vital societal interests that outweigh individual desires for digital erasure. This perspective holds that maintaining comprehensive digital archives promotes governmental and corporate accountability, preserves accurate historical records, and upholds fundamental principles of information freedom essential to democratic societies.

Transparency and Accountability in the Digital Age

The most powerful argument against RTBF legislation lies in its potential to shield powerful actors—governments, corporations, and public figures—from accountability for their actions. When information can be systematically removed from public access, the historical record becomes malleable, susceptible to revision by those with the resources and motivation to sanitize their past. This concern is not hypothetical; it strikes at the very heart of how societies hold power to account.

Consider the investigative journalist or human rights activist who documents corruption, environmental violations, or human rights abuses. If the subjects of such investigations possess the legal right to erase this documentation from the internet, the evidentiary foundation that enables public scrutiny dissolves. A politician's past statements, a corporation's previous safety violations, or a public figure's historical controversial actions all become erasable at the request of those who have most to lose from transparency. The result is a chilling effect on documentation and journalism, as the permanence of published information has historically served as a deterrent against misconduct precisely because wrongdoers know their actions become part of an indelible record.

The accountability function extends beyond high-profile figures to ordinary citizens who may need to access information about those with whom they entrust their safety, finances, or welfare. Employers, landlords, and community members often rely on publicly available information to make informed decisions. While individual privacy deserves protection, the collective interest in maintaining information ecosystems that enable verification and background-checking serves societal safety. Removing the ability to research an individual's history—whether to verify credentials, check for patterns of behavior, or simply understand who one is dealing with—creates information asymmetries that can harm the very people RTBF legislation claims to protect.

Historical Preservation and Collective Memory

Beyond accountability, permanent digital records serve an essential function in historical preservation. Human societies have always struggled with the tendentious nature of historical documentation, and the digital age offered unprecedented potential to create comprehensive, searchable archives of human activity. RTBF legislation fundamentally threatens this potential by introducing systematic gaps into the historical record, gaps that may be strategically placed to serve particular interests.

The preservation of accurate history matters for numerous reasons. Academic research depends on access to primary sources and documentary evidence. Legal proceedings require documentation of past events. Social movements learn from historical patterns of success and failure. Communities maintain their collective identities through shared remembrance of past events. When legislation enables the systematic removal of information from these archives, future generations inherit a distorted view of the past—a view shaped not by what actually happened but by what powerful actors wished to have remembered.

This concern becomes particularly acute when considering institutional memory. Governments, organizations, and movements often seek to rewrite their histories, emphasizing achievements while minimizing controversies or failures. RTBF legislation provides legal mechanisms for such revisionism. A government that committed human rights violations can request the removal of documentation. A corporation responsible for environmental disasters can seek erasure of media coverage. A religious institution accused of misconduct can remove records of accusations. In each case, the ability to erase historical documentation serves the interests of the powerful at the expense of collective memory and historical accuracy.

The historical argument against RTBF also encompasses what might be called the "right to remember." Just as individuals may wish to be forgotten, communities and societies have interests in remembering events that others wish to erase. Victims of abuse may want documentation of their experiences preserved. Historians studying particular periods require access to materials that subjects of study might prefer removed. Future researchers investigating societal patterns need comprehensive datasets rather than selectively curated ones. The RTBF framework, by prioritizing individual erasure requests over collective preservation interests, tilts the balance in ways that may impoverish our understanding of the past.

Information Freedom and the Public's Right to Know

The deepest philosophical objection to RTBF legislation concerns its fundamental tension with principles of information freedom. A free society depends on the free flow of information; citizens require access to facts, data, and perspectives to make informed decisions about their governance, their relationships, and their lives. RTBF legislation introduces state-sanctioned censorship into the digital information ecosystem, creating legal mechanisms for removing speech from public discourse based on the preferences of the subject rather than any determination of falsity or harm.

This framing matters because it reframes the RTBF debate from one of individual privacy protection to one of information control. The legislation does not simply protect individuals from false information; it enables the removal of accurate information that individuals find inconvenient or embarrassing. The implications for free expression and public discourse are significant. When information can be legally erased at the request of the subject, the internet becomes less a space of collective knowledge and memory and more a territory subject to the preferences of those who appear in its records.

The information freedom argument also encompasses concerns about private actors wielding power typically associated with governments. While RTBF legislation is typically enacted by states, its enforcement often targets private platforms like search engines and social media companies. These entities become de facto arbiters of what information remains accessible, subject to legal pressure and removal requests. The resulting chilling effect extends beyond direct legal requirements; platforms anticipating removal requests may proactively remove content to avoid liability, leading to over-censorship that suppresses legitimate speech and information sharing.

Furthermore, the global nature of the internet creates jurisdictional tensions that RTBF legislation exacerbates. European RTBF rules may remove information visible to European users while leaving it accessible elsewhere, fragmenting the global information space into zones of differing accessibility. This fragmentation serves neither information freedom nor the public's right to know, instead creating a patchwork system where truth varies by geography and where those with the most aggressive erasure regimes can effectively impose their preferences on global discourse.

The Practical Challenges of Implementation

Beyond these philosophical concerns, RTBF legislation faces significant practical challenges that undermine its beneficial claims while creating new problems. The fundamental difficulty lies in defining the scope and boundaries of what can be forgotten. Is information about a decades-old criminal conviction erasable while information about a similar recent conviction remains public? How do we balance an individual's interest in forgetting against the public's interest in knowing about patterns of behavior? What happens when multiple individuals are connected to the same event—does one person's erasure request remove information relevant to others' histories?

These questions admit no easy answers, and the practical result is often inconsistent application, creating winners and losers based not on the merits of erasure claims but on the resources and sophistication of those making requests. Wealthy individuals and large corporations can navigate complex legal processes; ordinary individuals often cannot. The result may be a system that primarily serves those with the most resources to exploit it, potentially including those who least deserve the protection of erased histories.

The global nature of information compounds these difficulties. Information removed from European servers may remain accessible through servers in other jurisdictions. The cats-and-mouse game between erasure and re-publication consumes resources without achieving the complete erasure that RTBF implies. Meanwhile, the existence of such mechanisms may create perverse incentives, encouraging individuals to behave badly with the expectation that unfavorable information can later be legally removed.

Acknowledging Legitimate Privacy Concerns

This argument against RTBF legislation does not dismiss legitimate privacy concerns. Individuals genuinely suffer from the permanent availability of information that no longer reflects their current circumstances or character. People rehabilitated from past mistakes deserve opportunities to move forward without constant association with historical errors. Young people who made foolish decisions before developing mature judgment face consequences disproportionate to their actions when that information remains perpetually accessible. These concerns are real and deserving of sympathetic response.

However, the response to these legitimate concerns need not be RTBF legislation. Alternative approaches include enhancing individual control over information visibility without removal from underlying databases, developing reputation systems that weight recent information more heavily than historical information, creating pathways for contextualizing past information with current circumstances, and strengthening protections against the malicious use of accurate but outdated information. These approaches address privacy concerns while preserving the information ecosystems that serve transparency, historical preservation, and information freedom.

Conclusion: Balancing Competing Values

The debate over the Right to be Forgotten ultimately involves balancing competing values that cannot be easily reconciled. Individual interests in controlling one's digital identity and moving forward from past mistakes must be weighed against collective interests in transparency, historical accuracy, and information freedom. This essay has argued that the balance should tilt toward preserving permanent records because accountability, historical preservation, and information freedom serve fundamental societal interests that individual privacy claims—however sympathetic—do not outweigh.

This conclusion does not mean that all information should remain permanently accessible regardless of context. Defamation law, privacy torts, and protections for vulnerable populations provide mechanisms for addressing genuinely harmful speech without the blunt instrument of RTBF legislation. The goal should be targeted responses to specific harms rather than broad frameworks that enable systematic erasure of accurate information by those who prefer it not exist.

A society that cannot remember its past cannot learn from it. A society that cannot hold power accountable enables its abuse. A society that surrenders control over its information ecosystem to the preferences of those who appear in it sacrifices the free flow of ideas that enables democratic governance. These are the stakes in the RTBF debate, and they argue for preserving the permanent record of human activity that the internet, for all its problems, has nonetheless made possible.

In Defense of Historical Information: The Case Against 'Right to be Forgotten' Laws

Introduction

The 'Right to be Forgotten' (RTBF) has emerged as a contentious legal concept that enables individuals to request the removal of personal information from online platforms and search engines. While proponents argue it protects privacy and allows people to move beyond their past mistakes, this essay firmly contends that such laws fundamentally undermine core democratic principles: the public's right to information, historical accuracy, and freedom of expression. Unrestricted access to historical information, even when unflattering to individuals, serves crucial societal functions that outweigh the privacy concerns RTBF laws aim to address.

The Threat to Historical Accuracy

RTBF laws create an unprecedented mechanism for the selective editing of our collective digital record. When individuals can legally remove unflattering yet factual information about their past activities, we compromise historical integrity. Consider a politician who successfully removes evidence of past controversial statements, or a business executive who erases records of prior fraudulent activities. The public is left with an incomplete, sanitized version of reality.

Unlike traditional privacy protections, RTBF enables the retroactive manipulation of already-published, factually accurate information. This represents nothing less than historical revisionism conducted through legal means. Archives, whether physical or digital, have traditionally been considered sacrosanct repositories of our shared history—RTBF laws fundamentally challenge this principle by declaring that historical accuracy is subordinate to individual discomfort.

The Public's Right to Know

Democratic societies function best when citizens have access to complete information about matters of public interest. This principle extends to information about individuals whose actions affect others—whether they are public officials, business leaders, or professionals serving the public. RTBF laws create concerning information asymmetries, where those with resources to pursue takedown requests can effectively scrub their digital footprints while the average citizen cannot.

For example, when consumers research professionals or businesses, they reasonably expect access to comprehensive information about past misconduct, legal troubles, or questionable practices. RTBF laws interfere with this legitimate interest, potentially hiding information crucial for informed decision-making. Similarly, voters deserve complete access to politicians' histories to make informed electoral choices. The erasure of unflattering but truthful information directly undermines this democratic function.

Freedom of Expression and Press Freedom

At its core, RTBF pits privacy rights against freedom of expression and press freedom. When we compel search engines or platforms to remove lawfully published information, we effectively censor speech after the fact. This represents a troubling expansion of censorship powers that extends beyond traditional defamation or privacy law.

Traditional press freedoms include the right to publish truthful information of public interest without fear of censorship. RTBF laws create a mechanism for retroactive censorship that chills journalistic freedom and inhibits the crucial watchdog function of the press. When journalists know their reporting may be effectively buried through RTBF requests, their incentive to pursue public interest stories diminishes.

Practical Implementation Problems

Even if one accepted the principle behind RTBF laws, their implementation raises insurmountable practical challenges. Who decides what information merits removal? Search engines and platforms become de facto arbiters of the public record, making consequential decisions about what information remains accessible—typically through opaque processes with minimal accountability.

The inevitable inconsistency in enforcement creates a patchwork approach to information access. Content may be removed in one jurisdiction while remaining available in others, creating information disparities based on geographic location. This fragmentation undermines the global nature of the internet and creates troubling precedents for jurisdictional control over worldwide information access.

Better Alternatives Exist

The legitimate concerns RTBF advocates raise—such as protecting individuals from outdated or irrelevant information—can be addressed through less restrictive means. Time-based archiving policies, improved search algorithms that prioritize recency and relevance, and context labeling present alternatives that preserve access while addressing legitimate concerns.

Rather than enabling removal of information, we should focus on contextualization. For instance, news organizations can update stories with subsequent developments, and platforms can facilitate the addition of context to older content. These approaches address the core concerns of RTBF advocates without compromising on historical accuracy or information access.

Conclusion

While privacy concerns in the digital age are legitimate, RTBF laws represent a dangerous overcorrection that prioritizes individual discomfort over collective rights to information and historical accuracy. A society that allows the retroactive erasure of inconvenient truths loses something fundamental: reliability of its historical record and the accountability that comes with persistent information.

Instead of legally mandated forgetting, we should embrace solutions that enhance context while preserving access to historical information. The path to addressing digital age privacy concerns cannot run through the deliberate creation of memory holes in our shared informational heritage. A truly democratic society requires unfettered access to its own history—unflattering truths and all.

This essay argues that unrestricted access to historical online information should prevail over individual requests to erase past records.

Historical and Epistemic Value

Online information constitutes our era's primary historical record. Once deleted, information becomes unavailable not just to current users but to future historians, researchers, and citizens. The European Union's GDPR right to erasure has already erased countless records—creating irreplaceable gaps in our collective memory. Journalists, academics, and watchdogs rely on accessing past statements, articles, and documentation. Allowing systematic deletion corrupts the historical record permanently.

Accountability and Public Interest

Public figures and institutions rely on institutional memory to face scrutiny. A politician's deleted controversial statements, a corporation's removed safety complaints, or a public figure's erased misstatements all undermine accountability mechanisms. Transparency advocates rightfully argue that power requires exposure of past conduct.

The Contradiction of Selective Memory

"Right to be forgotten" laws are inherently asymmetrical: powerful institutions can afford legal teams to remove damaging information while ordinary people cannot. Wealthy individuals and corporations exploit these laws to curate personal narratives, while documentation of their past actions disappears. This creates information privilege.

Chilling Effects on Public Discourse

If people believe their statements will be permanently deletable on request, this perversely encourages less careful public speech. Currently, knowing statements are permanent creates accountability. Erasure rights weaken the consequences that encourage responsible speech.

Serious Internal Tensions and Counterarguments

However, this position faces legitimate challenges worth acknowledging directly:

The Non-Consensual Exposure Problem

The strongest objection involves information posted about people without consent—intimate photographs, false accusations, addresses of abuse survivors. The right to be forgotten originated largely from cases involving intimate videos and harassment. Dismissing all claims as "accountability concerns" conflates:

  • Public records (court documents, legislative voting)
  • Newsworthy information (genuine public interest journalism)
  • Harassing or revenge content (inherently privacy-violating)

These genuinely differ. A principled argument for information preservation should distinguish them.

The Permanence Asymmetry

Digital information's permanence is historically unprecedented. Pre-internet, information naturally decayed through physical degradation and limited distribution. Now, a youthful mistake lives forever in search results, affecting employment, relationships, and safety in ways past generations never faced. Treating digital permanence as identical to historical preservation mistakes their fundamentally different character.

The Power Dynamics Problem

My earlier point about asymmetrical power actually cuts both ways: powerful actors also benefit from permanent documentation. But individuals with less institutional power face disproportionate harm from permanent searchability. A 19-year-old's mugshot appearing in every job search differs meaningfully from corporate accountability.

Rehabilitation and Proportionality

Societies have long recognized that people change. Criminal justice systems typically don't publicize juvenile records. The question becomes: should digital information enjoy less privacy protection than pre-digital records specifically received? That seems backwards.

Rather than unconditionally defending unrestricted access, a stronger position distinguishes categories:

Preserve Information for:

  • Government records and legislative actions
  • Newsworthy public events
  • Academic and research purposes
  • Institutional accountability documentation
  • Information explicitly in public interest

Allow Some Removal Conditions For:

  • Personally identifying information in non-newsworthy contexts
  • Intimate content shared without consent
  • Information with no legitimate public interest
  • Content demonstrably inaccurate or misleading
  • Clear harassment or safety threats

Implement Through:

  • Delisting rather than deletion (information remains archived but unsearchable)
  • Contextual framing (noting when information is historical rather than current)
  • Time-based access restrictions
  • Authentication requirements for sensitive searches

This approach preserves historical integrity and accountability while acknowledging legitimate privacy concerns.

The strongest case against blanket "Right to Be Forgotten" laws emphasizes that transparency and historical preservation serve democracy and justice. Allowing systematic erasure of past records creates dangerous gaps in public knowledge and enables evasion of accountability.

However, the most intellectually honest version of this position acknowledges that:

  • Not all online information deserves equal protection
  • Digital permanence differs from natural historical decay
  • Some personal information genuinely shouldn't be permanently searchable

Against the “Right to Be Forgotten”: Why the Public Record Must Remain Public

The so-called “Right to be Forgotten” is often presented as a humane response to the permanence of the internet. Its advocates argue that people should not be indefinitely haunted by old mistakes, embarrassing incidents, minor convictions, financial troubles, or unflattering news reports. That concern is understandable. Yet turning it into a legal power to remove truthful, lawfully published historical information is profoundly misguided. A legal right to erase or conceal the past threatens freedom of expression, undermines public accountability, distorts the historical record, and grants private individuals—and ultimately governments—dangerous authority over what society is permitted to remember.

Truthful information does not become illegitimate merely because it is old, inconvenient, or damaging to someone’s reputation. Once information has lawfully entered the public record, the public should remain free to find, examine, discuss, and preserve it. The proper response to an uncomfortable past is context, explanation, forgiveness, and rehabilitation—not state-mandated forgetting.

The Public Has a Right to Remember

A free society depends not only on the right to speak, but also on the right to receive information. “Right to be Forgotten” laws invert this principle. They treat access to truthful historical material as a presumptive injury and allow the subject of that material to demand that it be hidden from others.

But information about the past is not the exclusive property of the person it concerns. A newspaper report about a court case belongs to the historical record. A public statement belongs to those who heard and relied upon it. A report about professional misconduct may matter to former clients, future employers, researchers, journalists, voters, and members of the affected community. No individual should possess a retrospective veto over other people’s ability to access such material.

This principle is especially important online. Search engines, digital archives, and databases do not merely circulate gossip; they provide the indexing infrastructure through which modern society retrieves its collective memory. Removing a search result may not destroy the original document, but it can make that document practically invisible. In an age of overwhelming information, de-indexing is often erasure in all but name. A record that technically exists but cannot reasonably be found has been functionally suppressed.

Freedom of expression is therefore inseparable from freedom of discovery. The state should not force an archive, publisher, or search provider to conceal truthful public information simply because its continued availability is unwelcome to the person described.

History Must Not Be Rewritten by Its Subjects

Reliable history depends upon the preservation of records created before anyone knew how later events would unfold. If people can remove inconvenient parts of their public past, the resulting record ceases to be history and becomes reputation management.

Historical understanding is cumulative. A decades-old article that appears insignificant today may become essential when viewed alongside later events. An old business failure may reveal a pattern of conduct. A forgotten political speech may expose a public figure’s shifting principles. A minor regulatory action may become relevant to later professional misconduct. Even ordinary local news can be valuable to genealogists, social historians, legal scholars, journalists, and future generations.

No authority can reliably determine in advance which facts will remain important. A record that seems “irrelevant” now may acquire great relevance later. That is why preservation must be the rule. Decisions about historical significance should emerge through open inquiry, not through private deletion requests adjudicated by platforms, bureaucrats, or courts.

There is also something inherently troubling about allowing the subject of a record to decide whether the record deserves to survive. Historians do not permit rulers to edit archives because old documents embarrass them. Journalists do not allow interview subjects to revoke accurate quotations years after publication. Courts do not rewrite prior judgments merely because a party dislikes the reputational consequences. Digital records should receive the same protection.

Accountability Requires Durable Memory

Accountability is impossible without memory. People and institutions behave differently when they know that accurate records of their conduct will remain accessible. Permanent public information creates incentives for honesty, care, and responsibility. Legally enforced obscurity weakens those incentives.

This does not mean that every past mistake should define a person forever. It means only that no one has a legal entitlement to prevent others from knowing that the mistake occurred. Rehabilitation and erasure are not the same thing. A person can explain that an event happened long ago, show that circumstances have changed, present evidence of subsequent good conduct, and ask others to judge fairly. That process respects both personal growth and historical truth.

By contrast, removal laws manufacture an artificial form of innocence. They do not prove that the underlying information was false or unfair. They simply make it harder for others to discover. The result is not genuine redemption but information asymmetry: the subject knows the history, while those making decisions about trust, employment, business, leadership, or public responsibility may be denied access to it.

Such asymmetry can cause real harm. Consumers may wish to know whether a professional has faced past disciplinary action. Investors may need to examine the prior failures of company directors. Voters may want to compare a candidate’s current claims with earlier positions. Journalists investigating patterns of misconduct must be able to connect scattered events over time. Public access to historical information allows people to make their own judgments rather than relying on a legally sanitized presentation.

Legal Erasure Inevitably Becomes Subjective and Arbitrary

“Right to be Forgotten” regimes usually depend on vague standards such as whether information is outdated, irrelevant, excessive, or no longer in the public interest. These terms conceal difficult value judgments. Irrelevant to whom? Outdated for what purpose? Excessive according to which cultural standard? In the public interest as determined by what official, company, or tribunal?

There is no neutral answer. A ten-year-old record may seem irrelevant to the person seeking removal but highly relevant to an investigative reporter. A minor offense may appear trivial in isolation but important when it forms part of a broader pattern. A personal bankruptcy may be old news to one reader and material information to a potential business partner. The very premise of erasure requires someone to decide what other people are allowed to consider.

In practice, these decisions are often delegated to private technology companies. That is an extraordinary form of privatized censorship. Platforms faced with large numbers of complaints and the threat of legal liability have strong incentives to remove first and ask questions later. They cannot conduct a full historical, legal, and journalistic investigation into every request. Over-removal is therefore not an accident; it is the predictable result of the system.

The process is also structurally one-sided. The subject of an article has a strong personal incentive to seek removal, while the public interest in preserving access is diffuse. The original journalist may no longer be employed, the publisher may lack the resources to contest the request, and future researchers do not yet know that the hidden record exists. The person demanding concealment is present and motivated; the people who may someday need the information are absent and unrepresented.

Erasure Rights Favor the Powerful

Although these laws are often defended with sympathetic examples involving ordinary people, the tools they create are especially useful to those with money, influence, and legal assistance. Politicians, executives, professionals, public personalities, and wealthy litigants have far greater ability to identify damaging material, file repeated requests, hire specialists, and pressure publishers or platforms.

The result can be a two-tiered historical record. The powerful receive curated digital biographies, while those without resources remain fully exposed. A law supposedly intended to protect human dignity can become a mechanism for reputation laundering.

This danger extends beyond individuals. Once society accepts that truthful public information may be legally hidden because it causes reputational harm, governments and institutions gain a ready-made justification for suppressing their own embarrassing histories. The language of privacy can be stretched to cover corruption, incompetence, abuse, and misconduct. The boundary between personal dignity and public censorship will always be contested, and the institutions with the greatest power will be best positioned to push that boundary in their favor.

Open archives provide a defense against such manipulation. They allow journalists and citizens to bypass official narratives and examine what was actually said, reported, filed, or decided at the time.

Public Availability Is Not a New Wrong Merely Because Search Is Efficient

Supporters of removal laws often argue that the internet has transformed privacy because old records are now much easier to find. That is true, but greater accessibility does not make truthful information illegitimate. Libraries became more searchable through catalog systems. Court records became easier to examine through indexes. Newspaper archives became more useful when placed on microfilm and later digitized. In each case, improved retrieval increased the practical value of existing information.

It would be perverse to treat efficient access as a reason to suppress knowledge. Search technology corrects an old inequality: historically, only governments, large institutions, wealthy researchers, and well-funded journalists could afford to investigate extensive archives. Online access allows ordinary people to do the same. Restricting search results does not restore some natural condition of privacy; it restores the advantage of those with the time and resources to search manually.

A fact should not be available only to specialists. If a record is legitimately public, then the general public should be able to locate it without hiring an investigator or traveling to a distant archive. Formal openness combined with practical invisibility is not meaningful transparency.

Privacy Should Not Become Ownership of Facts

Privacy is an important value, but it should not be confused with ownership of all information relating to oneself. People do not possess a general property right in facts about their public actions. Others may remember those actions, document them, discuss them, and draw conclusions from them.

Once a truthful event has been lawfully observed and reported, it becomes part of more than one person’s experience. A business dispute belongs to both parties. A public proceeding belongs to the legal system and the community. A political controversy belongs to the electorate. A published interview belongs to the publisher and its readers as well as the interviewee. Allowing one participant to erase the record disregards everyone else’s interest in it.

The strongest privacy protections should focus on preventing wrongful collection, intrusion, surveillance, identity theft, and unauthorized disclosure of genuinely confidential material. They should not create a retrospective power to suppress truthful information that was lawfully public. False statements can be answered through correction and defamation principles. Fraud, harassment, threats, and unlawful access can be addressed directly. But truthfully documenting public events should not become illegal merely because time has passed.

Context Is Better Than Concealment

The most persuasive argument for forgetting is that old information can be misleading when stripped of context. A youthful offense, dismissed charge, old debt, or decades-old controversy may give an incomplete picture of the person today. Yet deletion is a poor answer to lack of context because it replaces an incomplete truth with a deliberate absence.

The better solution is more information. Archives can preserve follow-up reports. Search systems can display dates prominently. Publishers can attach corrections, acquittals, reversals, later developments, or statements from affected people. Individuals can publish explanations and evidence of rehabilitation. Institutions can adopt fair decision-making rules that limit how much weight should be placed on remote events. Society can cultivate norms of proportionality and forgiveness.

These responses preserve truth while reducing unfairness. They allow people to change without pretending that the past never happened. A mature society should be capable of distinguishing between remembering an event and condemning someone forever for it.

Indeed, legal erasure may undermine forgiveness. Forgiveness requires knowledge of what occurred and recognition of what changed. When the past is hidden, observers cannot evaluate growth; they can only encounter a manufactured blank space. Real rehabilitation is more credible when it coexists with an honest record.

The Risk of Abuse Outweighs the Promise of Relief

No doubt permanent online information can cause pain. Some people will be judged unfairly, and some old events will receive more attention than they deserve. But laws suppressing accurate public records do not eliminate human unfairness. They merely transfer power from readers and citizens to regulators, judges, and corporations.

That transfer carries enormous risks. Removal standards expand. Precedents accumulate. Platforms become cautious. Archives become incomplete. Researchers cannot know what has disappeared. Journalists lose leads. Citizens receive sanitized search results without realizing that material has been withheld. The public record is altered quietly, one request at a time.

Censorship is no less serious because it is fragmented and bureaucratic. A missing book on a library shelf is visible; a de-indexed result may leave no trace. The user sees an apparently complete account and has no way to measure the omissions. This invisibility makes digital suppression especially dangerous.

The law should therefore favor preservation, access, and transparency. It should not recognize a general entitlement to remove truthful historical information from public reach. People may request corrections, publish responses, seek mercy, demonstrate reform, or criticize the prominence given to old events. They should not be able to compel society to forget.

Conclusion

The “Right to be Forgotten” is appealingly named but wrongly conceived. Forgetting is a human process, not a legal entitlement to control collective memory. The law can protect people from lies, unlawful surveillance, threats, and genuine invasions of confidential life without granting them authority to suppress truthful public history.

An open society must accept that freedom of information sometimes produces discomfort. Public records may embarrass, complicate, and challenge. That is not a defect in transparency; it is part of its purpose. Historical information allows citizens to test claims, uncover patterns, hold institutions accountable, understand change, and resist manipulation.

Truth does not expire. Public facts should not become legally inaccessible simply because they are old or inconvenient. The answer to an unforgiving culture is greater fairness and context, not an official machinery of forgetting. Searchable archives and durable public records should remain open to everyone, free from compelled removal. Society should defend the right to remember—not create a right to rewrite the past.

RTBF frameworks typically empower institutions—sometimes courts, sometimes regulators, sometimes intermediaries—to decide that certain information must be removed from search results or even deleted from platforms. This matters because the internet is not just another medium; it is the primary index to public life. 2) It undermines the principle that public records belong to the public

The heart of the argument against RTBF is simple: if information was lawfully made public—through courts, elections, government actions, regulatory filings, or responsible journalism—it becomes part of the public record. Public records serve collective purposes: oversight, historical inquiry, civic accountability, and informed decision-making.

When RTBF laws treat those records as something individuals can unilaterally “clear” from digital visibility, they weaken the idea that the public—not just the subject of the record—has an ongoing right to know. Even if an event is old, public interest can persist for reasons such as:

  • pattern detection (e.g., repeated misconduct, serial fraud)
  • evaluation of current role suitability (e.g., public office, leadership positions)
  • research and watchdog reporting
  • verification of claims in new controversies

Supporters of RTBF sometimes claim the aim is not to erase facts but to remove “irrelevant” or “disproportionate” links from search results. However, this is a semantic compromise that masks a deeper issue: it empowers the legal system to manage collective memory.

The Tyranny of Oblivion: Why “Right to Be Forgotten” Laws Undermine Truth, Accountability, and Freedom

In an age when information is the oxygen of public life, a growing number of jurisdictions have begun to institutionalize a right to oblivion. Under various “right to be forgotten” (RTBF) regimes, individuals may petition search engines and data controllers to delist or erase links to lawfully published, truthful, and historically significant information about themselves. Ostensibly designed to protect privacy and dignity in a digital age, these laws in practice constitute a dangerous legal mechanism for rewriting history, shielding the powerful, and corroding the epistemic foundations of open societies. The Historical Record as Public Infrastructure

History is not a private diary; it is a commons. Societies depend on accessible records to understand patterns of behavior, assess institutional performance, and enforce norms over time. Journalists, historians, scholars, and ordinary citizens rely on the ability to retrieve and cross-reference information that was once public. This is especially true in the digital era, where much of modern life—financial transactions, professional conduct, political speech, and legal proceedings—leaves an electronic trail. To allow individuals to suppress links to that trail is to permit the selective bleaching of the historical record.

Consider a public official who once accepted improper payments, a doctor disciplined for malpractice, or a financier implicated in fraud. Years later, search results about these events may be inconvenient to their rehabilitation or rebranding. Under RTBF, they can demand that search engines suppress access to lawful reporting on these facts. The result is not privacy but distortion. The original articles remain online in principle, but the pathways to them are severed, rendering truth functionally invisible. This is not the correction of error; it is the curated forgetting of fact.

Moreover, RTBF regimes are structurally biased toward the already powerful and well-connected. Ordinary citizens rarely have the legal resources, time, or technical sophistication to file and sustain delisting requests. Corporations, politicians, and celebrities do. The effect is predictable: laws sold as tools of individual empowerment become instruments of elite reputation management, allowing the influential to launder their pasts while the public is left with a fragmented, manipulated archive.

Truth Is Not Subject to Consent

One of the most pernicious premises of RTBF is that individuals possess a quasi-proprietary interest in facts about themselves. This confuses privacy—an appropriate limit on intrusion—with control over historical truth. If a newspaper lawfully reports on a crime, a court proceeding, or a public statement, the resulting information enters the public domain. That it concerns an individual does not grant that person the right to retroactively veto its discoverability. A society that respects truth must accept that some truths are unwelcome.

This becomes especially acute in cases involving public interest. Whistleblowers, investigative journalists, and anti-corruption advocates rely on the permanence of records to hold power to account. When RTBF allows corporate executives or government officials to suppress links to past misconduct, it chills exposure and incentivizes silence. The message to those who might expose wrongdoing is clear: even if today’s revelations are lawful and accurate, tomorrow’s algorithms may bury them under a legal erasure request. In such an environment, accountability is temporally contingent, not morally or factually grounded.

Furthermore, RTBF’s focus on search engines rather than source material creates a façade of transparency. By permitting the underlying information to remain but rendering it unfindable, the law creates a Potemkin village of openness. Readers may falsely assume that if nothing appears in search results, nothing occurred. This epistemic void is more insidious than outright censorship because it masquerades as technical neutrality. It outsources historical judgment to algorithmic compliance and legal intermediaries rather than to the informed scrutiny of the public.

Slippery Slopes into Compulsory Amnesia

The definitional boundaries of RTBF are inherently unstable, and its logic invites continual expansion. Initially framed around outdated, irrelevant, or embarrassing personal data, delisting regimes have quickly broadened to encompass professional missteps, public statements, and even lawful journalism deemed “disproportionate” relative to an individual’s current standing. This elasticity reflects a deeper philosophical error: the belief that dignity requires the perpetual management of one’s historical footprint.

But human dignity does not require historical amnesia; it requires truthfulness, proportionality, and fairness. If a person has changed, that transformation can and should be documented by new facts—not by the artificial suppression of old ones. The proper response to a past mistake is not deletion but context: follow-up reporting, commentary, and the accumulation of a fuller record over time. RTBF short-circuits this process by privileging an individual’s desire to escape over the public’s right to remember and evaluate.

Once such a principle is enshrined in law, the pressure to extend it is relentless. Advocates already argue for broader interpretations that would allow delisting of non-personal but reputationally damaging material, such as negative reviews or historical corporate scandals. Some have even proposed applying RTBF retroactively to digitized archives and library holdings. Each step chips away at the integrity of the historical record, replacing stable memory with negotiated forgetfulness. The endpoint is not privacy, but a legal right to narrative control.

The Global Fragmentation of Truth

RTBF also creates a fragmented and jurisdictionally unstable information environment. A delisting order issued in one country may be invisible to users within that jurisdiction but remain accessible elsewhere, creating a splintered reality where truth becomes geographically contingent. For multinational companies and globally relevant figures, this invites forum shopping and legal arbitrage, as litigants seek the most favorable venues for erasure.

Search engines, in turn, are forced to act as private arbiters of history, making complex judgments about relevance, public interest, and proportionality under threat of legal penalty. These are decisions that, in free societies, should be entrusted to editorial judgment, historical scholarship, and public discourse—not to compliance departments responding to takedown notices. By outsourcing historical gatekeeping to corporate legal teams, RTBF enlists private intermediaries as censors, undermining both transparency and legitimacy.

Alternatives to Erasure: Reinforcing, Not Rewriting

The legitimate concerns that animate RTBF—outdated information, disproportionate harm, and the permanence of digital mistakes—should be addressed without undermining historical truth. Robust data protection laws can limit the collection and retention of unnecessary personal data going forward. Expungement regimes can clear legal records after rehabilitation. Journalistic ethics and libel law can correct errors and mitigate unwarranted harm. None of these requires the legal suppression of truthful, publicly available information.

Where information is accurate and lawfully published, its discoverability is not a bug but a feature of an open society. The answer to the discomfort caused by the past is not erasure but education: teaching individuals and institutions to engage critically with history, to distinguish between who someone was and who they are, and to accept that progress does not require denial.

Conclusion: A Society That Remembers Is a Society That Is Free

“Right to be forgotten” laws masquerade as protections for individuals while functioning as tools of historical revisionism. They privilege personal convenience over public knowledge, power over accountability, and present reputation over past truth. In allowing the legal removal and suppression of publicly available records, these laws normalize a regime of curated forgetfulness that weakens journalism, distorts history, and undermines democracy.

An open society must be a remembering society. It must insist that lawful, truthful information about the past remains accessible, searchable, and subject to scrutiny. To do otherwise is to surrender the future to those with the power to rewrite the past. The choice is stark and unambiguous: we must reject the right to be forgotten and defend, without compromise, the right to remember.
